s1: On the Moon, a broken wrench is not a small problem. The next one is three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres away, and sending it can cost up to a million dollars per kilogram.
s2: In 2026, NASA Glenn grew a plastic inside bacteria and mixed it with simulated Moon and Mars dust: a material that could be made on site. But which mix? How much dust, which dust, and is it strong enough for a wrench? You can't test every combination on Earth.
s3: For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we built the Moon-Material Simulator. Pick a binder, a soil, and how the part is made. Instantly, a physics model corrected by machine learning predicts eight properties, shows how sure it is, and tells you whether each number is backed by real lab data. It runs in any browser, and it's open source.
s4: Our science stands on NASA's own data: NASA Glenn's 2026 bacterial-plastic reports, NASA Kennedy's regolith-printing studies, and a 2003 NASA report on polyethylene and regolith, plus peer-reviewed papers. We transcribed 1,470 measured values, each tied to its page, table, row and column. Then we built an auditor that finds every number again in the original PDF. It never edits data; it only comments. Zero transcription errors, and 181 problems inside the papers themselves.
s5: Physics alone isn't enough: on real samples, its compressive-strength predictions were off by up to 230 percent. So we kept the physics and taught a Gaussian process its mistakes, using 152 real measurements from seven studies. On mixes it never saw, the error drops from 230 to 34 percent for compressive strength, 65 to 19 for stiffness, 16 to 5 for density. A completely new study is harder, and we say so. And every prediction links to its evidence: this one says 117 megapascals. The paper measured 119.
s6a: Back to our wrench: bacterial plastic with 38 percent lunar highlands dust. The part test applies beam theory to the model's predictions. It breaks at 71 newtons, just short of the 72 needed to tighten a bolt. At lunar noon it softens to a sixth of that. At lunar night it's almost twice as strong, but brittle: it snaps instead of bending.
s6b: So we ask the optimizer. It tests nearly five thousand mixes and finds one made entirely from local resources: 45 percent dust and 15 percent basalt fibre. Safety factor 1.7, and it bends before it breaks.
s6c: Ask it for a rocket nozzle, and it honestly says no plastic survives. And a kit of 25 small parts printed on site keeps 10 kilograms off the launch pad: up to 10 million dollars.
s7: Every kilogram made on the Moon is a kilogram we don't have to launch. Our simulator helps engineers choose the right mix before a single sample is printed, and shows which real measurement backs every answer. The same method works for Mars, and for any material where data is scarce. We are Dreams of X. Try it yourself.
